items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.

items.title: Depreciation methods change reported profit, not cash
items.claim: A delivery van costs £40,000 with a 4-year useful life and £8,000 residual value. Under straight-line depreciation, what is the year-1 depreciation charge?
items.reveal_title: Straight-line: (cost minus residual) divided by life
items.reveal:
(£40,000 - £8,000) / 4 = £8,000 per year. Reducing balance would front-load the charge (e.g. 40% of £40,000 = £16,000 in year 1).

Neither method affects cash flow — the van was paid for upfront. Depreciation is an accounting allocation that matches cost to revenue across periods, governed by IAS 16. Different methods produce different reported profits in early years but the same total over the asset's life.
items.why: Profit figures are sensitive to accounting policy choices. Cash flow is not. This is one reason cash flow statements were made mandatory under IAS 7.

items.title: Herzberg's hygiene factors don't motivate
items.claim: Frederick Herzberg's 1959 'Motivation to Work' surveyed 200 engineers and accountants. What did he conclude about pay?

options.text: Pay is a 'hygiene factor' — low pay causes dissatisfaction but high pay does not produce sustained motivation. Motivators are achievement, recognition and the work itself
Pay had no effect either way
Only senior staff are motivated by pay

items.reveal:
Herzberg's two-factor theory splits job factors into hygiene (pay, conditions, supervision, policies) — whose absence causes dissatisfaction — and motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) — which actively drive engagement.

Methodological critics note Herzberg used the 'critical incident' interview technique, in which people tend to attribute good experiences to themselves and bad ones to external factors. Replications using other methods get less crisp results.
items.why: Pay rises buy off dissatisfaction, not loyalty or effort. Most modern HR practice combines compensation (hygiene) with job design (motivators) — a direct legacy of Herzberg.
